q: Covalent bonding can occur between similar or even ____ atoms.
e: Diatomic molecules like $O_2$ and $N_2$ are formed by covalent bonds between identical atoms.

q: The concept of electron ____ rather than electron transfer explains bonding between similar or identical atoms.
e: Atoms with similar electronegativities share electrons rather than transferring them.

q: As a result, a covalent bond is formed by sharing one or more pairs of ____ electrons between atoms.
e: Only valence electrons are involved in the sharing that creates covalent bonds.

q: Thus, the covalent bond is the electrostatic attraction between the ____ of the atoms and the shared electrons.
e: The shared electron pair is simultaneously attracted to the positive nuclei of both bonding atoms.

q: Covalent bonding usually occurs between ____.
e: Non-metals have high electronegativities and ionization energies, favoring electron sharing.

q: If two hydrogen atoms are approaching one another, ____ forces act on the atoms at the same time.
e: The forces include electron-electron repulsion, nucleus-nucleus repulsion, and nucleus-electron attraction.

q: These three forces are (1) ____ force between the electrons of atoms since like charges repel, (2) attractive force between the nucleus of each atom and the electrons of another, and (3) repulsive force between the two positively charged nuclei.
e: Electrons on different atoms repel each other due to their identical negative charges.

q: When the hydrogen atoms are too close to each other, the ____ interaction between two nuclei becomes so strong that it pushes them apart.
e: Nuclear repulsion dominates at very short internuclear distances, preventing atoms from merging.

q: Consequently, there is an optimum distance between two nuclei called the ____ where net attractive forces are maximised and the most stable covalent bond is formed in the H-H molecule.
e: Bond length represents the equilibrium distance where potential energy is minimized.

q: In covalent bonding, the outermost orbitals of the atoms ____ so that unpaired valence electrons in each of the bonding atoms can be shared, whereas the paired valence electrons are not involved in bonding.
e: Orbital overlap is necessary to allow electron density to be shared between two nuclei.

q: By overlapping orbitals, the outer shells of all the bonding atoms are filled with valence electrons by following the ____ rule.
e: The octet rule drives atoms to share electrons until they have eight valence electrons.

q: The covalent bonds can be single bonds or ____ covalent bonds, namely double bonds and triple bonds.
e: Multiple bonds involve sharing more than one pair of electrons between the same two atoms.

q: In single covalent bonds, only ____ pair of electrons is shared between two atoms.
e: A single bond consists of exactly one shared electron pair (two electrons).

q: The length of the bond is determined by the number of ____ electrons.
e: More shared electrons pull the nuclei closer together, shortening the bond.

q: The higher the number of bonded electrons, the stronger the attraction between the two atoms and the ____ the bond length.
e: Triple bonds are shorter than double bonds, which are shorter than single bonds.

q: In contrast, the bond strength of the triple bond is the ____, followed by the double bond and single bond.
e: Sharing three pairs of electrons requires the most energy to break, making it the strongest bond.

q: A ____ bond, or dative bond, is a special type of covalent bond.
e: Coordinate bonds are formed when both shared electrons originate from the same atom.

q: This bond is characterised by the fact that the two shared electrons are both ____ by one of the participating atoms.
e: In a coordinate bond, one atom acts as the sole donor of the electron pair.

q: A coordinate bond is formed when one of the participating atoms possesses an unshared pair (a ____ pair) of electrons.
e: A lone pair is required to be donated to an empty orbital on the accepting atom.

q: This lone pair is donated to an atom needing them to build up, or complete, a stable electron octet or ____.
e: Hydrogen and helium aim for a duplet (two electrons) rather than an octet.

q: A coordinate bond is expressed as an ____, $ightarrow$ which indicates the direction in which the electrons are donated.
e: The arrow points from the donor atom to the acceptor atom.

q: The ammonia molecule possesses a lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom; it can be donated to a hydrogen ion to produce the ____ ion $NH_4^+$, forming a coordinate bond.
e: Ammonia acts as a Lewis base, donating its lone pair to $H^+$ to form the ammonium ion.

q: Similarly, a water ($H_2O$) molecule that possesses two lone pair electrons on the oxygen atom can react with a hydrogen ion, $H^+$, through a coordinate bond, giving a ____ ion, $H_3O^+$.
e: Water donates a lone pair to a proton to form the hydronium ion in acidic solutions.

q: In addition, molecules with incomplete octets, called ____ molecules, can accept an electron pair from a molecule bearing a lone pair.
e: Molecules like $BF_3$ lack a full octet and act as Lewis acids.

q: In carbon monoxide, the CO molecule has a triple bond that consists of two covalent bonds and one ____ bond where both electrons come from the O atom.
e: Oxygen donates a lone pair to carbon to satisfy carbon's octet in CO.

q: Lewis structures are only ____-dimensional representations of how the valence shell electrons are arranged around individual atoms in a molecule or an ion.
e: Lewis structures are flat drawings and do not show the actual 3D geometry of molecules.

q: In a Lewis structure, a covalent bond is described by writing each shared electron pair either as a pair of two dots between symbols of two atoms or as a ____ connecting them.
e: A single line represents one shared pair of electrons (a single bond).

q: Some molecules that deviate from the octet rule, such as electron-deficient molecules and ____ valence shell molecules can occur.
e: Elements in period 3 and below can use d-orbitals to accommodate more than eight valence electrons.

q: The central atom in an electron-deficient molecule has valence electrons of ____ than 8, and that in an expanded valence shell molecule has valence electrons of more than 8.
e: Boron and beryllium commonly form stable compounds with fewer than eight valence electrons.

q: The molecular shape in which the atoms and electron pairs exist in a ____-dimensional arrangement can be predicted by using the Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion (VSEPR) theory.
e: VSEPR theory predicts the 3D geometry of molecules based on electron pair repulsion.

q: This theory is a model in chemistry used to predict the ____ of covalent molecules.
e: Molecular shape determines many physical and chemical properties of a substance.

q: It is based on the idea that the three-dimensional geometry of a molecule is mostly determined by the ____ interactions of the electron pairs around a central atom.
e: Electron pairs repel each other and arrange themselves to be as far apart as possible.

q: This model assumes that the electron pairs will arrange themselves to ____ repulsion effects from one another.
e: Minimizing repulsion leads to the lowest energy, most stable molecular geometry.

q: The repulsive interaction of electron pairs increases in the order of bonding pair-bonding pair < lone pair-bonding pair < ____.
e: Lone pairs occupy more space and exert the greatest repulsive force on other electron domains.

q: The lone pairs are ____ on the central atom while each bonding pair is shared between two atoms.
e: Because lone pairs are attracted to only one nucleus, their electron cloud spreads out more.

q: These lone pairs of electrons in a molecule occupy ____ space compared with the bonding pairs of electrons.
e: The greater spatial requirement of lone pairs compresses the bond angles between bonding pairs.

q: All diatomic molecules represent two points in space and are joined by a straight line, i.e., they are ____.
e: Any molecule with only two atoms must be linear by definition.

q: As shown in Table 1.1, a triatomic molecule ($AX_2$ type) has a ____ shape.
e: An $AX_2$ molecule with no lone pairs on the central atom adopts a 180° linear geometry.

q: In this type, it has only two bonding pairs without ____ pairs.
e: The absence of lone pairs allows the bonding pairs to spread to the maximum 180° angle.

q: Thus, the shape of $BeCl_2$ is ____.
e: Beryllium chloride is an electron-deficient linear molecule.

q: In the $CO_2$ molecule, there are ____ bonding pairs (two double bonds) without lone pairs.
e: Each double bond counts as one effective electron domain, but consists of four shared electrons.

q: If the lone pair is present in these types, the molecular shapes are not the ____ as the geometry of electron pairs.
e: Molecular shape only considers atom positions, while electron geometry includes lone pairs.

q: For example, $AX_3$ has a triangular planar and $AX_2E$, where E represents a lone pair, has a ____ (bent).
e: The presence of a lone pair pushes the bonding pairs closer together, creating a bent shape.

q: Some elements occur in solids where the atoms are held together by single covalent bonds, existing as ____ structures.
e: Giant covalent structures form extensive networks of covalent bonds throughout the entire crystal.

q: For example, in a diamond, each carbon atom is joined to ____ other carbon atoms by strong covalent bonds, and the carbon atoms form a regular tetrahedral network resulting in a giant structure.
e: Carbon in diamond is $sp^3$ hybridized, forming four single bonds.

q: There are no ____ electrons.
e: All valence electrons in diamond are localized in covalent bonds, making it an insulator.

q: In the case of graphite, it has a layer and planar structure formed by joining each carbon atom to the other ____ carbon atoms by covalent bonds.
e: Carbon in graphite is $sp^2$ hybridized, forming three bonds in a planar hexagonal lattice.

q: Each layer is formed with ____ rings of carbon atoms.
e: The planar sheets of graphite consist of fused six-membered carbon rings.

q: There are weak ____ forces between the layers, which give rise to a giant structure.
e: Weak van der Waals forces allow the layers of graphite to slide over one another.

q: In contrast to diamond, graphite has ____-moving electrons in each layer.
e: The unhybridized p-orbitals in graphite form a delocalized pi-system of free electrons.

q: That is why graphite can ____ electricity.
e: The delocalized electrons can move freely along the planes, allowing electrical conduction.

q: Silicon(IV) oxide, $SiO_2$ (silica or quartz) is an example of a ____ covalent molecule.
e: Silica forms a continuous 3D network similar to the structure of diamond.

q: In quartz, each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms, but each oxygen atom is bonded to only ____ silicon atoms.
e: The 1:2 ratio of Si to O is maintained by each oxygen bridging two silicon atoms.

q: The oxygen atoms are formed as ____ between the tetrahedrally bonded silicon atoms.
e: Oxygen acts as a bridge connecting the $SiO_4$ tetrahedra into a giant lattice.

q: It does not ____ electricity because it has no free moving electrons.
e: Like diamond, all electrons in silica are tightly bound in covalent bonds.
